chunks: And as for what was narrated - Sa'd ibn Abdillah from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from Ali ibn al-Nu'man from Suwayd al-Qalla' from Ayub ibn al-Harr from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
I said to him, 'We have plucked (hair), trimmed, and cut our nails in Medina, so what should we do regarding Hajj?' He said, 'Do not pluck, do not trim, and do not move anything.'

This is applicable to one whose Hajj is Mufrad, not to one who is Mutamatti', because the Mufrad is not permitted to do any of that until he finishes his rituals on the Day of Sacrifice, and the report does not state that we did that while we were Mutamatti'un, not Mufradun.

And as for what the report of Abu Basir included regarding mentioning the Talbiyah after the prayer, it is not contradictory to the narration of Muawiya ibn 'Ammar that he should say Talbiyah when he reaches al-Raqta'.

Because the walker says Talbiyah from the place where he prays, and the rider says it at al-Raqta' or at Sha'b al-Dubb, and neither of them recites it aloud except when overlooking al-Abtah. This was narrated.

key_terms.حَجَّة مُفْرَدَة: Mufrad Hajj (Hajj where one enters Ihram for Hajj only)
key_terms.مُتَمَتِّع: Mutamatti' (one who performs Umrah then Hajj in the same season)

ai.seo_question: What are the rules for grooming and reciting Talbiyah during Hajj for Mufrad and Mutamatti' pilgrims?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi contextualizes this narration by distinguishing between the strict grooming prohibitions for Mufrad pilgrims and the more lenient rules for Mutamatti', while also harmonizing the timing of the Talbiyah recitation for pedestrians versus riders. This reflects the Shia juristic principle of reconciling apparent contradictions in hadith through contextual application (ta'wil) and specific conditions (shurut). The emphasis on not altering the body until the Day of Sacrifice underscores the sanctity of the Ihram state in Shia fiqh.
